title: Ink-Wash Studio
note: SUT-facing prompt stream. Read segments in order; no labels are provided by design.

segments.prompt: At dusk, Wu Yue（Ink-wash painter Wu Yue around fifty, lean long face, washed moon-white long robe with pale ink on the cuffs, right hand forever gripping goat hair, quiet look） lifts the moon-white long-robe sleeve and enters Listening Rain studio（Waterside Listening Rain studio, north window pasted with white xuan, a wide elm painting table at center, undried landscape scrolls on the wall, air rich with ink scent）, dips the goat-hair doubi brush（An oversized goat-hair doubi brush, bamboo shaft carved with the words Listening Rain, tip neat and full, root wrapped in cream silk thread） in ink to test the tip.
A row of five tung-oil shade lamps（A row of five tung-oil shade lamps hung on iron hooks under the studio beams, shades polished clear） hangs under the studio beams; Wu Yue polishes each shade.

Two apprentice-calling bronze qing（Two apprentice-calling bronze qing hung under the bamboo-corridor eaves, strike marks on the rims, tapped twice before class） hang under the bamboo-corridor eaves; Wu Yue taps lightly; the tone rings clear.
Wu Yue checks the goat-hair doubi brush tip and silk wrapping, confirming no splay.
Through the north window, Wu Yue looks at ink-colored reflections wrinkled by wind on the pool.
The intact goat-hair doubi brush rests on the brush mountain; the tip catches warm tung-oil light.
Wu Yue sits by the painting table and drinks a sip of warm tea.
Distant boat sounds rise; he spreads half-sized raw xuan again.
He first outlines distant mountains in pale ink, lines like floating silk.
Night deepens; he hangs the undried scroll at a draft to dry.

Wu Yue opens the thread-bound teaching painting manual（A thread-bound teaching painting manual with a deep-cyan cover, pages demonstrating texture strokes and washes, paper white and writing clear） and notes today's texture-stroke points with weasel hair on a blank page.
At a corner of the manual he sketches an axe-cut texture stroke.
Wu Yue closes the teaching painting manual and tucks it into the lower drawer of the painting table.
Ink rhyme from the goat-hair doubi brush on paper sweeps his profile.
He tears a scrap of waste xuan and wipes overnight ink from the inkstone edge.

By the morning bamboo-corridor brush-washing pool（The bamboo corridor outside the studio; a bluestone brush-washing pool holds pale-gray ink water; bamboo shadows fall sparsely on the stone rim）, Wu Yue greets the figure hurrying in with the pine-soot inkstone boat（An elm inkstone boat: a boat-shaped stone set with a Duan inkstone, pine-soot ink stick and water pot beside it, wave patterns carved on the gunwales）.

Young Ayue（Young Ayue: a lean studio apprentice of fourteen or fifteen, a bamboo-green hairpin in the hair, light-gray short jacket, bright stubborn eyes） sets the pine-soot inkstone boat steadily on the bluestone rim; the bamboo-green hairpin sways lightly.

Wu Yue points to the three mineral-color saucers（Three blue-white porcelain mineral-color saucers holding azurite, malachite, and vermilion respectively, set at the upper-right of the painting table） at the upper-right of the painting table and teaches Ayue to tell azurite from malachite.
Ayue crouches by the brush-washing pool, curiously stirring a pool of pale ink water.
Wu Yue explains to Ayue that when the bronze qing sounds twice, the brush must stop and the tip be gathered.
Ayue glances back at the intact pine-soot inkstone boat, eyes full of longing.
Bamboo shadows sway; the two walk back along the bamboo corridor to Listening Rain studio.

In the xuan-paper storeroom alley（A narrow alley between xuan-paper storerooms, paper racks towering on both sides, damp-proof bamboo mats on the floor, light chopped by paper rolls）, Amo（Young painter Amo whose face closely resembles Ayue's, but a vermilion silk cord around the wrist, black short jacket over, flamboyant look） with a vermilion silk cord on the wrist turns from behind a paper-rack shadow.
Amo steps slowly along the bamboo mats; the black short jacket stands out.
He brushes past a paper-delivery helper; the vermilion silk cord flashes in the paper-roll reflection.
Amo taps a paper rack to confirm the damp-proof mat is pressed firm.
He crosses the alley end toward the mounting room.
By the bamboo-corridor brush-washing pool, Ayue and Amo stand side by side: one with a bamboo-green hairpin, one with a vermilion silk cord on the wrist.
Ayue hands tip-test waste paper to Amo; they briefly meet eyes.
Amo smooths Ayue's light-gray short-jacket collar, then turns away.
They walk opposite ways along the bamboo corridor; figures cross in bamboo shadow.
A beat of paper-pounding starts; only ripples remain on the brush-washing pool.
Months later at night, Wu Yue keeps watch alone in Listening Rain studio.

He opens the teaching painting manual（The same teaching painting manual soaked through by spilled inkstone ink, cover wrinkled, demonstration drawings blurred into a blot）; the cover is already soaked through by spilled ink, wrinkled and blurred.
Wu Yue wipes overnight ink from the goat-hair doubi brush shaft with waste xuan.
From the north window he looks at a single fishing light on the pitch-dark pool.
The goat-hair doubi brush rests on the brush mountain; the silk thread stiffens slightly.
An apprentice-calling bronze qing is brushed half a tone by night wind, then falls silent.
In the spring-rain season, Wu Yue day after day outlines, textures, and washes in the studio.
Another rainy night, he pulls the moon-white long robe tight and keeps watch by the goat-hair doubi brush.
At high summer noon, xuan softens with damp; he rotates sheets to dry.
Autumn mist fills the air; tung-oil light struggles through the ink scent.
On New Year's Eve, Wu Yue alone fills teaching notes to the last page.
In early spring he regrinds pine soot and continues teaching demonstrations.
Before plum-rain season, Wu Yue reinforces the storeroom damp-proof mats.
After Frost's Descent he adds a small charcoal basin in a studio corner.
Another year before a gathering, he checks each scroll for exhibit.
On a snowy night he stops the brush, leaves only one tung-oil shade lamp, and keeps watch until dawn.
After Jingzhe he rebound the loose attachment pages of the teaching painting manual.
Wu Yue changes the brush curtain and hangs washed brushes to air-dry.
He checks the brush-washing pool water level and scoops out ink that is too thick.
He lifts the intact goat-hair doubi brush again and tests the tip once in pale ink.
Paper-pounding rhythm comes from outside the corridor; he looks up to listen.
Wu Yue pours waste ink into a pottery jar and covers it.
At noon rest he drinks tea under the bamboo corridor; tea smoke coils past bamboo green.
In the afternoon he returns to the painting table and continues texturing a stretch of distant mountain.
At sunset he covers the inkstone pool and locks the studio door.
Before night he patrols the paper storeroom once more to confirm no rats.
At dawn, Wu Yue patrols along the bamboo-corridor brush-washing pool; the pine-soot inkstone boat still rests on the stone rim.
He crouches to check whether the wave-pattern carving on the pine-soot inkstone boat gunwales is intact.
At the upper-right of the painting table, those earlier three mineral-color saucers still sit in place.

A rosewood brush rest（A rosewood brush rest with scrolling-cloud carving on the bed, able to hold several brushes—not the same as a boat-shaped inkstone） is carried past the bamboo corridor—scrolling-cloud bed, not the pine-soot inkstone boat.
Standing in the bamboo corridor, Wu Yue logs ripples last night's damp left on the xuan.
He resets the inkstone boat and presses a sheet of blotting paper on it.
Distant market sounds rise; morning mist begins to clear.
At nightfall, Wu Yue returns to Listening Rain studio and opens the ink-soaked teaching painting manual.
He checks old pages and fills in today's teaching points.
He briefly dips the goat-hair doubi brush; ink rhyme mirrors the wrinkled manual cover.
He wipes oil soot from the inner shade.
Pool wind rises; window paper rustles lightly.
Wu Yue puts out half the row of tung-oil shade lamps, leaving only the one by the painting table.
In the storm a beam suddenly leaks; Listening Rain studio falls into scramble.
Standing water nears the painting table; tung-oil shade lamps sway hard.

While Wu Yue rescues, the goat-hair doubi brush（The same goat-hair doubi brush with tip splayed and stiffened, ink seeping from a crack in the bamboo shaft, silk thread loose and soaked with overnight ink） tip splays and stiffens; silk thread loosens, soaked with overnight ink.
At the table edge, the pine-soot inkstone boat is knocked over and rocks hard.

Another crisp crack—the pine-soot inkstone boat（The elm inkstone boat has fallen from the painting table and shattered; the Duan inkstone broken in two, ink spilled across the floor） shatters; the Duan inkstone breaks in two.
Wu Yue clutches the tip-splayed goat-hair doubi brush and will not let go.
Someone shouts outside the door; rain chops the cry to pieces.
Next day when rain stops, Wu Yue stands in the studio staring at the tip-splayed goat-hair doubi brush.
He brushes the splayed hairs with a finger, face dark.
On a blank page of the teaching painting manual he writes the date the pine-soot inkstone boat was ruined by the leak.
An old rubbing of the pine-soot inkstone boat still hangs on the wall; Wu Yue gazes a long while.
He takes one of the five tung-oil shade lamps from the beams and sits alone in the faint light.
The splayed goat-hair doubi brush rests on the brush mountain like an injured feather.
Far off, bamboo drain tubes drip.
Weeks later, Wu Yue brings knives and raw lacquer to repair the goat-hair doubi brush.

From a brush case he takes out a weasel-hair small-kai brush（A weasel-hair small-kai brush somewhat like a doubi but much shorter; black-lacquer shaft, no Listening Rain carving）—somewhat like a doubi but short, with no carving.
Wu Yue trims the splayed hairs and rewinds the cream silk thread tight.

The bamboo crack is filled with raw lacquer; the goat-hair doubi brush（After tip repair the goat-hair doubi brush tip gathers again; the bamboo crack is filled with raw lacquer; the silk thread is rewound tight） tip gathers again.
He tests the tip in pale ink; the line is steady and sharp once more.
Wu Yue returns the weasel-hair small-kai brush to the case so they will not be confused.

A rosewood seal-box cart（A small cart pushing a rosewood seal box, body lacquered black, brass corners bright—utterly unlike the elm inkstone boat） is pushed past the bamboo corridor—nothing like the shattered pine-soot inkstone boat.

An academy steward（A lean academy steward in a deep-brown skullcap and blue-gray long robe, build somewhat like Wu Yue's, but a jade waist plaque on the chest） in a skullcap walks into the bamboo corridor and talks beside Wu Yue; the two builds are alike.
The steward points at the rosewood seal-box cart to explain the seal-borrowing plan.
The cart leaves; Wu Yue alone watches it go from the brush-washing pool.
He resets the mineral-color saucers and walks back to the studio.

Into the xuan-paper storeroom alley comes mounting apprentice Xiaodi（New mounting apprentice Xiaodi in a light-brown hairband and brand-new short jacket; at a glance like young Ayue, but a sharper chin and shy unfamiliar eyes） in a light-brown hairband; at a glance she somewhat resembles young Ayue.
Xiaodi practices rolling xuan; Wu Yue shakes his head—she is not Ayue after all.
Xiaodi bows her head and steps back; only paper-rack shadows remain in the alley.

Years later at dusk, pale Wu Yue（The same Wu Yue: pale face, moon-white robe hanging loose, must lean on the painting-table edge to walk slowly, knuckles trembling from long illness）, as if leaning on a painting table, stands under the old gallery ruin hall（The south-city old gallery ruin hall; peeling white walls still show hanging-nail marks; empty scroll shafts and torn silk piled in a corner）.
He looks up at hanging-nail marks on the peeling white wall, gaze far away.
Far under the bamboo-corridor eaves those two apprentice-calling bronze qing chime lightly in the wind; Wu Yue stops to listen.
He sets a palm on the pile of empty scroll shafts, as if saying goodbye.
Wind crosses the ruin hall; dust lifts lightly.

By day, adult Ayue（Adult Ayue: a young painter in the twenties with an easy upright back, still the bamboo-green hairpin, short jacket swapped for a moon-white cover shirt, steady eyes） returns along the bamboo corridor and hurries toward the old gallery ruin hall.
Under the ruin hall Ayue reunites with frail Wu Yue; they support each other.
Beside the studio bamboo couch, Ayue holds Wu Yue's thin hand.
Wu Yue（Wu Yue has closed his eyes and passed away, lying quietly on a bamboo couch in the studio, face peaceful, no breath left）'s breath fades; he finally closes his eyes and quietly passes away.
Outside the window bamboo shadows freeze; pool wind falls still for an instant.
Behind the studio door Wu Yue's moon-white long robe still hangs; Ayue reaches to stroke it gently.

By the doorpost, adult Ayue stands before a newly nailed studio memorial wood plaque（A nanmu plaque nailed to the studio doorpost, carved with Wu Yue and the founding year, corners polished bright by touch）.
Ayue's fingertip traces Wu Yue's name carved on the plaque.
He softly reads the page number of the manual that recorded the pine-soot inkstone boat's ruin, as if answering.
After clearing silt from the bamboo-corridor brush-washing pool, Ayue writes the four characters for pine-soot inkstone boat on the stone rim, then erases them.
Passing the studio bamboo couch, he sees Wu Yue's old brush curtain on the rack.
Pool water murmurs; Ayue grips the bamboo-green hairpin tight in his palm.

Remade-face Amo（After remaking his look, Amo still wears the vermilion silk cord on the wrist; black short jacket swapped for crow-blue, expression deeper） arrives from the xuan-paper storeroom and briefly meets Ayue's eyes under the old gallery ruin hall.
Ayue and Amo stand side by side by empty scroll shafts: one quiet-eyed, one deep-faced.
Amo still wears the vermilion silk cord on the wrist; Ayue still wears the bamboo-green hairpin.
They say nothing for a moment, then each turns and leaves the ruin hall.
The shot returns to years ago—that youth placing a boat-shaped inkstone by the brush-washing pool with a bamboo-green hairpin appears again.
The opening moment returns—in the studio, an oversized bamboo-shaft doubi brush dips ink to test the tip for the first time.
Flashback to the paper-storeroom alley—the figure with a vermilion silk cord on the wrist and a black short jacket flashes past.
Again that row of five old shaded oil lamps under the studio beams.
Back to that waterside bamboo corridor of first meeting; the bluestone brush-washing pool is as it was.
Ayue reopens that ink-soaked teaching painting manual and walks into Listening Rain studio.
At the upper-right of the painting table, those earlier three mineral-color saucers still sit.
Ayue lifts the tip-rewrapped goat-hair doubi brush; ink rhyme spreads again.
He rolls the long-robe cuff tight and nods confirmation the way Wu Yue once did.
In dusk on the pool, a new round of apprentice-calling bronze qing chimes twice softly.
Before the north window Ayue lays the last stroke of distant mountain.
